title: US Pours $500M Into Critical Minerals as Goldman Warns Europe May Need €100 Gas for Winter; India Weighs Russian Crude Under Tariff Threat
subhead: Washington pumps half a billion into domestic battery minerals while Goldman warns Europe needs gas prices to double by December to fill winter storage. Iran and Oman meanwhile struck a temporary Hormuz corridor deal that pushed Brent to a two-week low.

sections.heading: Hormuz: Iran and Oman Agree Temporary Corridor, Oil Slips to Two-Week Low
sections.body:
Iran's Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi announced Tuesday that Tehran and Muscat have agreed on a temporary maritime route through the Strait of Hormuz, per Al Jazeera. The waterway will not fully reopen, he stressed, until the United States fulfills commitments under the June interim peace deal, which has since lapsed. The strait has been effectively closed since Iran shut it in early March, weeks after the US-Israel strikes on Tehran began on February 28.

Reuters reports Brent fell more than $2 a barrel to a two-week low near $86-87 as the talks revived hopes of easing shipping constraints, with some outlets showing losses around 3%. The agreement formalizes what had become a fractured two-route system: a southern course backed by Oman and the US, and a northern one Iran had designated for 'friendly' ships. About 20 percent of global oil and LNG transits the strait, roughly 130 ships a day in peacetime.
sections.whyItMatters: The corridor deal is de-escalation on paper but not a resolution — Iran keeps the strait as leverage while talks with the US remain frozen, so the market's relief is provisional.

sections.heading: Europe's Winter Gas Crunch: Goldman Sees €100/MWh Needed
sections.body:
Goldman Sachs analysts warned in a weekend note, carried by Bloomberg and Oilprice.com, that European benchmark gas at the Dutch TTF needs to move above €100/MWh by December for the continent to stock enough inventory for winter — some 110 percent above their €50/MWh base case. Europe is losing the competition for spot LNG to Asia, particularly with most Qatari term volumes unavailable.

Gas Infrastructure Europe data shows storage around 62 percent full, the lowest for this time of year in nearly two decades and well below the five-year average. TTF traded near €66.85 ($78)/MWh on Monday, far short of the level Goldman says would spur accelerated stockbuilding. European prices have roughly doubled over 2026, per Euronews.
sections.whyItMatters: The Middle East war has broken Europe's summer refill cycle — either prices spike toward €100 to pull in LNG, or the continent enters winter under-stocked, with 2022-style shortages a live risk.

sections.heading: Critical Minerals: DOE Deploys $500M to Break China's Grip
sections.body:
The US Department of Energy selected seven critical mineral processing, battery manufacturing, and recycling projects for a combined $500 million, according to Shale Magazine. Recipients include lithium-ion battery recyclers Princeton NuEnergy and Nth Cycle, per WasteDive, with funding arriving as new black mass export restrictions aim to keep recovered materials domestic.

Separately, the DOE finalized a nearly $1 billion loan for the contentious Rhyolite Ridge lithium mine in Nevada, a project central to domestic battery supply plans, Yahoo Finance reported.
sections.whyItMatters: Washington is moving from rhetoric to capital in the minerals race — recycling plus hard-rock lithium now sit alongside Chinese supply chains as the target, not just the talking point.

sections.heading: Russia Sanctions: Senate Bill Puts 100% Tariffs on India, China Over Russian Crude
sections.body:
The US Senate has passed a Russia sanctions bill that could expose the top five purchasers of Russian crude and gas — including India and China — to import tariffs of up to 100 percent, per Moneycontrol and ANI. The measure targets countries that keep buying Russian energy as Moscow's exports shift further from Western financial reach.

Indian refiners are meanwhile leaning more on Russia, the UAE, and South America for August crude amid West Asia supply disruptions, the Hindu BusinessLine reports, keeping New Delhi in the crosshairs. The sanctions architecture is tightening just as Russia-China trade hit a record $159.24 billion in the first seven months, with 99.1 percent of bilateral payments bypassing the dollar, largely settled in yuan and rubles via CIPS.
sections.whyItMatters: The bill turns secondary sanctions into blunt trade policy, threatening to drag India and China into an explicit tariff confrontation over energy choices — and exposing how little leverage dollar-based penalties now have over the Moscow-Beijing axis.

sections.heading: Nuclear Politics: Trump Sends Saudi Deal to Congress Without Enrichment Bar
sections.body:
President Trump has sent Congress a proposed 30-year civil nuclear agreement with Saudi Arabia that would allow US firms — chiefly Westinghouse, jointly owned by Cameco and Brookfield — to build AP1000 reactors worth tens of billions, Reuters and US News report. Trump insists the pact will only take effect if Riyadh normalizes relations with Israel under the Abraham Accords. Congress has 90 session days to review; rejection could be vetoed, requiring a two-thirds override.

Critics, including some Democratic lawmakers, note the deal does not bar Saudi enrichment or reprocessing — pathways the UAE forswore in its 2009 'gold standard' pact. The Trump administration says legally required nonproliferation measures are included.
sections.whyItMatters: Sending a nuclear deal without an enrichment ban to Congress, tied to Israel normalization, pits nonproliferation norms against a strategic realignment — and hands Saudi Arabia a civilian nuclear platform with weapons-adjacent potential.

sections.heading: China's Energy Plan: New 2030 Targets as De-Dollarized Trade Deepens
sections.body:
China released its 15th Five-Year Plan for the oil and gas sector on August 17, setting new 2030 targets for energy infrastructure development, Reuters reported. The plan lands amid the region's worst supply disruption in decades, with Asia most exposed to Gulf shipping constraints.

It also dovetails with accelerating financial decoupling: Russia-China trade hit a record $159.24 billion in seven months, up 26.3 percent, with 99.1 percent of bilateral payments now settled outside the US dollar via yuan, rubles and the CIPS system — the clearest evidence yet that major-economy trade can run outside Western sanctions reach, as MSN summarized.
sections.whyItMatters: Beijing is hardening its domestic energy infrastructure while its trade with Moscow deepens outside the dollar — a two-track hedge against the exact supply and financial shocks the current crisis keeps producing.

bottomLine: The day's energy map is defined by two diverging signals. On the supply side, Iran and Oman's temporary Hormuz corridor deal pushed Brent to a two-week low — but it is a managed de-escalation, not a reopening, and the strait stays Tehran's leverage. On the demand and policy side, Washington is spending $500 million on domestic critical minerals while the Senate moves toward 100 percent tariffs on Russian-crude buyers, and Goldman warns Europe may need €100/MWh gas to survive winter. The US-Saudi nuclear deal heads to Congress without an enrichment bar, and China locks in 2030 infrastructure targets as its trade with Russia exits the dollar. Underlying all of it: the Gulf crisis has made energy a weapon and a subsidy, and every major power is now buying insurance — in minerals, storage, routes, or financial plumbing.
sources: Al Jazeera, Reuters, Oilprice.com, Bloomberg, Gas Infrastructure Europe, US News, Shale Magazine, WasteDive, Yahoo Finance, Moneycontrol, ANI, Hindu BusinessLine, Euronews, MSN, Washington Examiner
